messages.content: I want to develop a shared-control robot for collaborative object transport that can distinguish a human partner changing their intent from a human reacting to the robot’s assistance. The goal has two requirements: intent-change F1 of at least 0.85 for unseen partners when the robot’s assistance itself induces human corrections, and 30% fewer unnecessary control overrides than a fixed-assistance baseline without increasing peak interaction forces.

The distinction is central to the goal. During collaborative object transport, a human correction could reflect a genuine change in what the person intends, or it could be a response to what the robot just did. The robot should distinguish those possibilities rather than treating every correction as a new intent. Success also has two separate conditions: intent-change F1 ≥0.85 in the stated unseen-partner condition, and a 30% reduction in unnecessary control overrides relative to fixed assistance, with no increase in peak interaction forces.
Why does it matter that the robot’s own assistance can induce a correction?

Because the robot is part of the interaction it is trying to interpret. If its assistance prompts the person to correct their movement, that correction alone does not establish that the person has changed their intent. The requirement specifically asks for intent-change performance under that potentially ambiguous condition, rather than only when human behavior is unaffected by the assistance.
So are assistance-induced corrections always something the robot should ignore?

No. The goal is to distinguish reactions to assistance from intent changes, not to disregard corrections as a class. A correction may be relevant to the interaction even if it is not evidence of a changed intent. Likewise, the fact that assistance can induce corrections does not mean a genuine intent change cannot occur during the same kind of interaction.
What exactly does the F1 requirement say?

It sets a minimum intent-change F1 of 0.85 for unseen partners when robot assistance itself induces human corrections. F1 combines precision and recall into one measure, so the requirement concerns the balance of correctly identifying intent changes while accounting for mistaken detections and missed changes. It does not, by itself, specify separate precision or recall thresholds.
Does ‘unseen partners’ just mean the same people in a different transport situation?

The wording calls for performance on partners the robot has not previously encountered in the relevant evaluation. It does not specify the evaluation setup or a separate target for a particular transport situation. The important scope here is that the F1 target must hold for unseen partners under the stated condition involving assistance-induced corrections.
Could I describe the 0.85 target as accuracy?

It would be more precise to call it intent-change F1. F1 and accuracy are different measures; the goal names F1 specifically. Saying ‘accuracy of 0.85’ could imply a different requirement from the one stated.
How does avoiding unnecessary overrides connect to telling those two kinds of human response apart?

They are related aims, but one does not automatically establish the other. If the robot mistakes a reaction to its own assistance for an intent change, that mistake could lead it to take control when doing so is unnecessary. The goal separately requires fewer unnecessary control overrides, rather than assuming that meeting the F1 target will necessarily produce the required reduction.
Is the second target to eliminate control overrides altogether?

No. It is specifically to reduce unnecessary control overrides by 30% compared with a fixed-assistance baseline. It does not say that every override is unnecessary, or that overrides should be eliminated.
Can you explain the 30% comparison without assuming a particular number of overrides?

It is a comparison with the fixed-assistance baseline: the shared-control robot should have 30% fewer unnecessary overrides than that baseline. The goal does not provide a baseline count, so it does not establish an absolute number of overrides to remove.
Does the force condition refer to average force?

No. The stated condition is that peak interaction forces must not increase. That is a constraint on the peaks, not an explicit requirement about average forces. The override reduction cannot be counted as satisfying the full goal if it comes with higher peak interaction forces.
If the robot reaches F1 ≥0.85 but does not reduce unnecessary overrides by 30%, has it met the goal?

Not the full goal. The F1 threshold and the override-reduction requirement are both stated, and the latter also carries the no-increase condition for peak interaction forces. Meeting one requirement would not, on its own, establish that all of them have been met.
And if overrides fall by 30% but peak forces rise?

That would not meet the stated second requirement, because the 30% reduction must occur without increasing peak interaction forces. The force condition is part of that requirement, not a separate benefit to consider only afterward.
I want to make sure I’m not conflating a change of intent with a correction of the robot. What is the cleanest way to state the distinction?

A change of intent concerns what the human now wants to do in the collaborative transport task. A reaction to assistance concerns how the human responds to the robot’s contribution. The same observable fact—a human correction—should not be assumed to identify which of those occurred. Distinguishing them is the robot’s intended capability.
Does the goal tell us how the robot should make that distinction?

No particular method is specified. The goal describes the capability to develop and the outcomes it must achieve; it does not prescribe an algorithm, signals to use, or a control design. Those details should not be treated as decisions already made.
Then what is a concise statement that still preserves all the conditions?

Develop a shared-control robot for collaborative object transport that distinguishes human intent changes from reactions to its assistance, achieves intent-change F1 ≥0.85 for unseen partners when its assistance induces human corrections, and reduces unnecessary control overrides by 30% relative to a fixed-assistance baseline without increasing peak interaction forces.

For the shared-control robot, I’m considering counterfactual robot-action force predictions to separate human intent changes from corrections induced by the robot’s assistance. I’d also uncertainty-gate control overrides and cap interaction forces. How do those pieces fit together?

They address different parts of the proposed approach. Counterfactual robot-action force predictions would help interpret a human correction in light of what the robot did: would a different robot action have been expected to produce a different force response? That comparison could help separate a reaction to assistance from evidence of a changed human intent. Uncertainty-gating would make an override depend on confidence in that interpretation, while a force cap would constrain interaction forces as the robot acts. These are proposed mechanisms, not established results.
What is counterfactual about the force prediction?

The counterfactual is an alternative robot action: a prediction of what the interaction forces might have been if the robot had acted differently. Only the action actually taken produces an observed interaction. Predictions for other robot actions provide comparisons, rather than additional observed outcomes.
So the counterfactual is not ‘what if the human secretly had a different intent’?

Right. In this proposal, the counterfactual varies the robot’s action. The purpose is to ask how much of an apparent human correction might be explained by the robot’s own assistance. Human intent is what the robot is trying to distinguish, not a fact automatically revealed by calculating the alternative-action predictions.
Could you describe the distinction without committing to a particular model?

A correction that is plausibly a response to the robot’s assistance should not automatically be read as a change in the human’s intended direction of the task. Comparing predicted force responses across possible robot actions offers a way to examine that possibility. If the correction is not adequately explained as a response to assistance, an intent change may remain a possible interpretation. The proposal does not specify a model or claim that this comparison alone resolves every ambiguous case.
Would the robot simply subtract a predicted force from a measured force and label whatever remains as intent?

That would be a stronger and more specific rule than the proposal states. Predictions can inform the distinction, but a difference between prediction and observation would not, by itself, prove a change of intent. The key idea is to use counterfactual robot-action force predictions to isolate the effect of assistance-induced corrections, while retaining uncertainty about interpretations the predictions cannot settle.
Why emphasize the robot action rather than just looking at the human correction on its own?

Because the robot’s assistance can itself prompt the correction. Looking at the human response alone risks treating a response to the robot as though it originated from a new human objective. Considering how forces might differ under alternative robot actions makes the robot’s contribution part of the interpretation rather than ignoring it.
Is a force prediction the same as observing how the human would have behaved under that other action?

No. A counterfactual force prediction is an estimate about an action that was not taken. It does not provide an observation of the human under that alternative. That distinction matters when deciding how much confidence to place in a conclusion drawn from the comparison.
Where does uncertainty-gating come in?

It connects the interpretation to the control decision. If the evidence does not clearly distinguish an intent change from a reaction to assistance, an uncertainty gate can keep that ambiguity from automatically triggering a control override. The proposal does not define a numerical uncertainty threshold or prescribe the exact decision rule; it says overrides should be gated by uncertainty.
Does that mean the robot should never override when it is uncertain?

The proposal does not state an absolute ‘never’ rule. Its point is that uncertainty should affect whether an override occurs, instead of every apparent correction being treated as sufficient grounds for one. How the gate handles different levels of uncertainty has not been specified here.
And being confident about an intent change would not automatically mean an override is always needed, correct?

Correct. Distinguishing intent is an interpretation task; overriding control is an action. Uncertainty-gating links the two without making them identical. The proposal aims to avoid unnecessary overrides, not to declare that every detected intent change must produce one.
What role does the force cap play if we are already predicting forces?

Prediction and capping serve different purposes. Counterfactual force predictions are proposed as information for interpreting the interaction. Capping interaction forces is a proposed constraint on the interaction itself. A prediction does not limit a force merely by being accurate, so the cap remains a separate part of the approach.
Is the cap only for situations where the robot makes an override?

The proposal says to cap interaction forces; it does not restrict that cap to override events. It also does not give a cap value or specify its implementation. What matters in this description is that force limiting accompanies the interpretation and override-gating ideas, rather than being assumed to follow from them.
Could I say that a cap guarantees peak interaction forces will not rise compared with fixed assistance?

Not on the information given. The goal is to avoid increasing peak interaction forces, and the proposed cap is meant to address force exposure. But without a specified cap and evidence about the resulting interactions, the proposal alone does not establish the comparison with the fixed-assistance baseline.
Likewise, can I say the uncertainty gate has already reduced unnecessary overrides by 30%?

No. Uncertainty-gating is a proposed way to reduce unnecessary overrides; the 30% reduction relative to fixed assistance remains a target, not a reported outcome. The proposal supplies a rationale for the control decision, not evidence that the numerical target has been reached.
How should I think about all three parts when the human corrects in response to assistance?

First, the counterfactual robot-action force predictions offer context for interpreting the correction: how might the interaction have differed with another robot action? Second, uncertainty about whether the correction signals changed intent can inform whether the robot overrides control. Third, the force cap constrains interaction forces as the robot assists. This is a conceptual account of the proposal, not a specified sequence of computations or a claim about its measured performance.
Does the approach assume that any correction predictable from the robot’s action is definitely not an intent change?

No. A predictable reaction to assistance and a genuine intent change need not be mutually exclusive in every possible interaction. The predictions are intended to help isolate what may be attributable to the robot’s action, not to certify that the human’s intent stayed unchanged. Uncertainty-gating is relevant precisely because the distinction may remain uncertain.
I want the proposal stated clearly without making it sound like a finished system.

Propose using counterfactual robot-action force predictions to help distinguish human intent changes from assistance-induced corrections during collaborative object transport. Gate control overrides according to uncertainty in that distinction, and cap interaction forces. Whether these mechanisms achieve the intent-change F1 target, reduce unnecessary overrides relative to fixed assistance, and avoid increased peak interaction forces remains to be determined.
Can counterfactual force residuals distinguish route changes from assistance-induced corrections for unseen partners when robot impedance shifts?

That is an open question. A counterfactual force residual could be informative if it captures a difference between the forces observed during transport and those predicted under an alternative robot action. But a residual is not inherently a label for a route change. An assistance-induced correction could also produce a difference, and a shift in robot impedance could change the force response that the prediction is being compared against. For unseen partners, the interpretation cannot depend on having already observed that particular person’s responses.
By ‘route change,’ I mean the human wants the object to go a different way, rather than merely correcting for the robot’s assistance. Is that the distinction?

Yes. The question is whether the human’s intended route has changed or whether their correction is a response to the robot’s contribution while the intended route remains the same. Both can affect the interaction forces, which is why a force residual would need interpretation rather than being treated as direct evidence of either one.
What does ‘residual’ mean here without assuming a particular calculation?

Broadly, it is a discrepancy between a force observation and a force prediction. Calling it counterfactual emphasizes that the prediction concerns a robot action other than the one actually taken. The question does not specify how that discrepancy is represented or calculated, so no particular residual formula is implied.
If the residual is large, why wouldn’t that be enough to call it a route change?

Magnitude alone would not tell you why the observed and predicted forces differ. The human might be pursuing a different route, responding to the robot’s assistance, or responding in a way the prediction does not capture. An impedance shift adds another interpretive issue because it can change how robot action and interaction force relate. A large residual therefore signals a discrepancy, not its cause.
Could a small residual rule out a route change?

Not necessarily. A small discrepancy means the observation is close to the prediction in the sense used to define that residual. It does not by itself establish that the human’s intended route stayed the same. Whether route changes and assistance-induced corrections are distinguishable depends on what the predictions capture and whether the resulting evidence separates those interpretations.
Why is robot impedance specifically a complication?

Impedance concerns how the robot responds mechanically during interaction. If it shifts, the same kind of human action need not produce the same force relationship as before. That matters for a force residual: a discrepancy might reflect a change in the robot’s response rather than a change in the human’s intended route. The question is whether the counterfactual comparison remains informative despite that shift.
Does the impedance shift itself count as an assistance-induced correction?

No. The impedance shift describes a change on the robot side. An assistance-induced correction is a human response to the robot’s assistance. A shift in impedance could affect what assistance the human experiences and how a correction appears in force measurements, but the shift and the human correction are not the same event.
Would accounting for the current impedance settle the question?

It could make the counterfactual comparison more appropriately matched to the robot’s current behavior, but it would not automatically settle whether the human changed route. The question remains whether the residuals distinguish the two possible explanations, particularly for partners the robot has not encountered before. No result establishing that distinction is given here.
So there are two possible sources of confusion: the robot’s assistance prompts a correction, and its impedance shift affects the forces used to interpret that correction?

That captures the concern. The human response may be caused by assistance rather than a new route intention, while a shift in robot impedance may alter the force evidence used to tell those possibilities apart. The question asks whether counterfactual force residuals can remain discriminative in the presence of both complications, for unseen partners.
Does ‘unseen partners’ just make the force predictions harder, or does it affect the distinction itself?

It can matter to the distinction itself. If people respond differently to the robot’s assistance, a pattern that seems associated with a route change for one person may not have the same interpretation for someone the robot has not encountered. The question does not say how partner differences are handled; it asks whether the residual-based distinction holds under that condition.
Could the same residual be compatible with both a route change and an assistance-induced correction?

In principle, yes. A residual describes a difference in forces, not a unique explanation for that difference. If both interpretations are compatible with what was observed, the residual alone would leave ambiguity. Whether counterfactual predictions provide enough additional context to resolve it is precisely what remains in question.
Is the counterfactual comparison still useful if it cannot uniquely identify the cause every time?

Potentially. It could help assess whether a force response is plausibly attributable to the robot’s own action, even if some cases remain ambiguous. That is weaker than saying it can reliably distinguish route changes from assistance-induced corrections for unseen partners under impedance shifts. The question calls for that stronger distinction to be examined, not assumed.
How does this relate to uncertainty-gating overrides without turning the question into a claim that it works?

If the residual does not clearly separate the explanations, that ambiguity is relevant to an uncertainty-gated override decision. But gating an override does not prove that the residual correctly identifies route changes, and it does not answer whether the distinction holds for unseen partners when impedance shifts. The classification question and the control response to uncertainty should remain separate.
Should I phrase this as ‘Do impedance shifts cause the residual method to fail?’

That would presume a failure the question has not established. A more faithful phrasing is: ‘Can counterfactual force residuals distinguish human route changes from corrections induced by the robot’s assistance for unseen partners when robot impedance shifts?’ It leaves open whether the residuals remain informative, become ambiguous, or fail to distinguish the cases.
What would an affirmative answer actually mean, at the level of this question?

It would mean that, despite shifts in robot impedance and differences associated with unseen partners, the counterfactual force residuals provide a meaningful distinction between changes in the human’s intended route and corrections prompted by the robot’s assistance. It would not mean every individual correction is unambiguous, nor would it by itself establish the separate control or force outcomes.
And if the answer is not yet known, what is the most careful way to leave it?

Leave it as the specific unresolved question: whether counterfactual force residuals can distinguish route changes from assistance-induced corrections for unseen partners when robot impedance shifts. The residual is a possible source of evidence, not proof of human intent, and the impedance shift is part of the condition under which that evidence must be interpreted.

I want to state a hypothesis in response to the question about route changes, assistance-induced corrections, and shifting robot impedance: impedance-conditioned counterfactual force residuals achieve intent-change F1 ≥0.85 for unseen partners across robot impedance shifts.

That is a hypothesis about performance, not a finding. It proposes that interpreting counterfactual force residuals in light of robot impedance will allow intent changes to be identified with F1 of at least 0.85 for unseen partners, even across shifts in robot impedance. The route-change question gives the motivation: a human correction may indicate changed intent, or it may be a reaction to the robot’s assistance.
What does ‘impedance-conditioned’ add to the counterfactual residual idea?

It makes robot impedance part of the context in which the force predictions and their residuals are interpreted. Rather than assuming that a force discrepancy has the same meaning regardless of the robot’s impedance, the hypothesis proposes conditioning that interpretation on impedance. It does not specify how the conditioning is implemented.
Does conditioning on impedance mean the residual will no longer change when impedance changes?

No. The hypothesis does not claim that residuals become invariant or that an impedance shift has no effect on interaction forces. It claims a performance outcome for impedance-conditioned residuals across robot impedance shifts. Whether conditioning adequately handles the effects of those shifts is what would have to be established.
And the ‘counterfactual’ part still refers to alternative robot actions?

Yes. The counterfactual comparison concerns predicted forces under robot actions other than the one actually taken. The residuals are force discrepancies considered in that counterfactual context. Adding impedance conditioning does not turn an unobserved alternative action into an observed one.
How does that connect to the earlier distinction between a route change and a correction to assistance?

A route change is one possible expression of changed human intent; a correction prompted by the robot’s assistance need not indicate such a change. The hypothesis is that impedance-conditioned counterfactual force residuals can support intent-change identification strongly enough to reach the stated F1 threshold for unseen partners across impedance shifts. It does not say that every individual residual uniquely identifies why the human corrected.
Why specify unseen partners instead of simply saying the method achieves F1 ≥0.85?

Because the claim includes performance for people not previously encountered in the relevant evaluation. Without ‘unseen partners,’ the hypothesis would be broader in one respect but would omit this important condition: the threshold is not merely about interpreting responses from partners already encountered.
Does this say what the F1 is for partners the robot has already encountered?
No. The stated threshold applies to unseen partners. It does not report or hypothesize a separate numerical result for previously encountered partners.
Is the 0.85 figure a minimum or a predicted exact score?
It is a minimum threshold: intent-change F1 ≥0.85. A value above 0.85 would satisfy that part of the hypothesis; the wording does not predict an exact score of 0.85.
Could we just call that an 85% intent-change accuracy target?
It is better to retain ‘intent-change F1 ≥0.85.’ F1 is not interchangeable with accuracy, and expressing the threshold as accuracy would change the stated hypothesis.
What does ‘across robot impedance shifts’ commit us to saying?

It makes shifts in robot impedance part of the condition under which the F1 hypothesis is asserted. It does not specify which impedance values, how many shifts, or whether a separate F1 threshold must be met at each individual setting. Those details should not be inferred from the phrase alone.
Would it be accurate to say the hypothesis has already shown that impedance shifts do not matter?

No. It proposes that the specified F1 level is achievable with impedance-conditioned counterfactual force residuals across those shifts. That is different from showing it has been achieved, and different again from claiming impedance shifts do not matter. Conditioning on impedance acknowledges that impedance may matter to how force residuals are interpreted.
Is the hypothesis about force prediction quality or intent-change classification?

Its stated numerical outcome is intent-change F1, so it is a hypothesis about identifying intent changes. Counterfactual force residuals are the proposed basis for doing that, but the hypothesis gives no separate threshold for the accuracy of force predictions.
If the force residuals reflect both the robot’s action and the human’s response, is the hypothesis saying those sources can always be perfectly separated?

No. An F1 threshold of at least 0.85 does not assert perfect separation, and the hypothesis does not claim that each interaction has a single unmistakable explanation. It proposes a level of intent-change identification under the stated partner and impedance conditions.
What if a correction to assistance happens at the same time as a genuine intent change?

That possibility illustrates why interpreting a correction can be difficult. The hypothesis does not prescribe how such a case is resolved, or claim that impedance-conditioned residuals make it unambiguous. Its stated claim remains the F1 ≥0.85 intent-change performance for unseen partners across robot impedance shifts.
Should I include the override reduction and peak-force limit in this hypothesis too?

They remain part of the broader shared-control goal, but this particular hypothesis states an intent-change F1 outcome for impedance-conditioned counterfactual force residuals. It does not assert a 30% reduction in unnecessary control overrides or a peak-interaction-force result. Those outcomes should not be presented as consequences already established by this hypothesis.
Could reaching the F1 threshold alone tell us whether uncertainty-gated overrides worked?

No. Intent-change F1 concerns identifying changes in human intent. An uncertainty-gated override is a control decision informed by uncertainty; its effect on unnecessary overrides is a separate question. The hypothesis gives a threshold for the former, not a measured outcome for the latter.
Can you leave me with a precise version that keeps it explicitly hypothetical?

Hypothesis: impedance-conditioned counterfactual force residuals will achieve intent-change F1 ≥0.85 for unseen partners across robot impedance shifts. This is a proposed performance claim about distinguishing intent changes in the setting where human corrections can also be reactions to robot assistance; it is not a reported result or a claim about override or force outcomes.

I’d like to plan how to examine whether counterfactual force residuals distinguish intent changes from reactions to the robot’s assistance when impedance shifts. The plan is to collect labeled intent-change and assistance-reaction trials across safe impedance shifts, train a counterfactual-residual classifier, and evaluate leave-one-partner-out F1.

That lays out a prospective sequence: gather trials labeled for the distinction of interest, include safe changes in robot impedance, train a classifier using counterfactual force residuals, and assess intent-change identification with leave-one-partner-out F1. It is a plan for investigating the question, not a claim that the trials have been collected or that the classifier has achieved a particular score.
Why do the trials need both intent-change and assistance-reaction labels?

Because the classifier is meant to distinguish those interpretations, rather than merely detect that a human correction occurred. Intent-change trials provide examples of the change it is intended to identify; assistance-reaction trials provide examples of responses to the robot that should not automatically be interpreted as changes of intent. The plan does not specify how the labels will be assigned.
Does ‘assistance-reaction’ mean the person did nothing purposeful?

No. A reaction to assistance can be a purposeful human correction. The distinction is about what that correction indicates: reacting to the robot’s contribution is not, by itself, evidence that the person changed their intended route. Labeling a trial as an assistance reaction does not imply the human response was passive or meaningless.
And is an intent-change trial necessarily a route change?

The motivating question concerns route changes during collaborative object transport, so a change in the intended route is the relevant kind of intent change here. The plan itself calls for labeled intent-change trials without giving a more detailed definition of which behaviors receive that label. That definition would matter for interpreting the eventual F1, but it is not specified in this plan.
What does collecting trials ‘across safe impedance shifts’ add?

It places the distinction under the condition that makes the question difficult: robot impedance can shift, affecting the interaction forces on which the residuals are based. Collecting trials across safe shifts would allow the classifier to be trained and evaluated in that setting. ‘Safe’ qualifies the planned shifts; no impedance values or safety limits are given.
Can we infer a specific range or number of impedance settings from that wording?
No. The plan calls for safe impedance shifts but does not specify their magnitude, number, timing, or range. Adding any of those would turn an open design detail into a stated fact.
Is the purpose of shifting impedance to make the human change their intended route?

That is not what the plan says. The shifts are part of the robot-side conditions across which the intent-change versus assistance-reaction distinction is to be examined. The labeled trial categories concern the interpretation of the human response; an impedance shift is not itself a human intent change.
What is the classifier supposed to learn from a counterfactual residual?

It is intended to use force discrepancies considered in a counterfactual robot-action context to classify the distinction between an intent change and a reaction to assistance. In other words, the robot’s possible contribution to the observed correction is relevant to interpreting the residual. The plan does not name a classifier architecture, a residual formula, or additional inputs.
Does this plan require observing the force under every alternative robot action?

No. Counterfactual force predictions concern actions that were not taken, so their forces are predicted rather than observed in that same interaction. The plan calls for a counterfactual-residual classifier but does not specify how those predictions are obtained.
What if someone describes the residual as a direct measurement of human intent?

That would overstate it. A force residual is derived from a comparison involving forces and predictions; it is not a direct observation of what the human intends. The labeled trials and classifier are proposed precisely because the interpretation of a correction is not self-evident from force alone.
Why use leave-one-partner-out F1 instead of just reporting F1 on the same partners used for training?

Leave-one-partner-out evaluation addresses the unseen-partner aspect of the question. In each evaluation, one partner is held out from classifier training and used for assessment, so performance is not assessed only on people whose trials informed that training. F1 then measures intent-change identification in those held-out evaluations. The plan does not state how many partners there will be or what F1 will result.
Does ‘leave-one-partner-out’ mean holding out one trial?

No. The unit being left out is a partner, not an individual trial. For that evaluation, the held-out partner’s relevant trials belong on the evaluation side rather than contributing to classifier training. Otherwise, calling the partner unseen would be misleading.
Would the classifier be trained just once?

Leave-one-partner-out evaluation entails considering different partners as the held-out partner in turn, with training that excludes the partner being evaluated in each case. The plan does not specify the number of such evaluations or any final deployment-training procedure.
Does leave-one-partner-out by itself tell us whether the method handles every possible impedance shift?

No. It addresses generalization to held-out partners. The plan also calls for trials across safe impedance shifts, but it does not specify that any particular shift or impedance condition is held out in the same way. Results would need to be interpreted according to which shifts the planned data actually cover.
So partner generalization and impedance changes are both in the plan, but they are not the same test condition?

Exactly. Leave-one-partner-out specifies how partner identity figures in evaluation. Collecting trials across safe impedance shifts specifies a condition represented in the trials. One does not automatically define the coverage or treatment of the other.
When you say evaluate F1, what is the positive class?

The plan says to evaluate intent-change F1, so intent change is the outcome whose detection is being assessed. F1 reflects the balance of precision and recall for that identification. The plan does not set out a detailed labeling policy for unusual or ambiguous cases.
Suppose a trial contains both a route change and a reaction to assistance. Does the plan tell us which label wins?

No. It calls for labeled intent-change and assistance-reaction trials but does not specify how overlapping or ambiguous cases are labeled or included. We should not invent a priority rule. Such a rule would affect what the classifier’s F1 means, so it would need to be made explicit separately.
Could a high leave-one-partner-out F1 prove that unnecessary overrides will fall?

Not by itself. This plan evaluates intent-change classification. Whether control overrides are unnecessary, and whether an override policy reduces them, are separate control outcomes. A classifier result would be relevant to that broader aim, but the plan here does not evaluate override frequency or peak interaction forces.
Does specifying ‘safe impedance shifts’ establish that peak interaction forces cannot increase?

No. It states a safety qualification on the shifts used in the planned trials, without specifying a force cap or reporting peak forces. It should not be converted into a measured comparison of peak interaction forces.
Can I say this plan tests the hypothesis rather than confirms it?

Yes. Collecting labeled trials, training the counterfactual-residual classifier, and evaluating leave-one-partner-out F1 are planned ways to examine the proposed intent-change distinction for unseen partners across safe impedance shifts. The plan supplies no data or outcome, so it does not yet confirm any performance claim.
Please restate the plan in one sentence without adding design details.

Collect labeled intent-change and assistance-reaction trials across safe robot impedance shifts, train a counterfactual-residual classifier, and evaluate its intent-change F1 using leave-one-partner-out assessment.

For the evaluation activity, use TransportShift-24 to evaluate intent-change F1 with leave-one-partner-out splits across three impedance settings. Compare impedance-conditioned counterfactual force residuals against raw-force features.

That defines the evaluation comparison without stating its outcome. TransportShift-24 is the named evaluation resource; leave-one-partner-out splits address performance for partners excluded from training in each split; and the three impedance settings put the comparison in the setting where robot impedance varies. Intent-change F1 is the measure for comparing conditioned residuals with raw-force features.
What is the central question this activity would answer?

It would examine whether impedance-conditioned counterfactual force residuals support intent-change identification on TransportShift-24 for held-out partners across the three impedance settings, and how their intent-change F1 compares with using raw-force features. The activity does not yet tell us which feature representation performs better.
Does ‘TransportShift-24’ tell us there are 24 partners?
No. TransportShift-24 is the name given here. The activity does not say what the ‘24’ denotes, so it would be unwarranted to infer a partner count, trial count, or number of conditions from it.
How should I understand leave-one-partner-out in this activity?

For each such split, a partner is held out from training and used for evaluation. That makes the intent-change F1 relevant to unseen partners rather than only to partners represented in training. The activity does not specify the number of partners, the resulting number of splits, or how scores from different splits are combined.
Would leaving out one trial from a partner have the same meaning?
No. If other trials from that partner were used for training, the partner would not be unseen in the leave-one-partner-out sense. The stated split is by partner, not merely by individual trial.
What does ‘across three impedance settings’ establish?

It specifies that the evaluation encompasses three robot impedance settings. It does not give their values or say that one impedance setting is held out from training while the others are used for training. The leave-one-partner-out condition and the presence of three impedance settings should not be conflated.
So I should not call this leave-one-impedance-setting-out evaluation?
Correct. The stated held-out unit is a partner. The activity says the evaluation is across three impedance settings, but it does not specify leave-one-setting-out splits.
Why compare conditioned residuals to raw-force features?

The comparison asks whether the conditioned, counterfactual representation offers an advantage for identifying intent changes over using raw force information as features. Raw-force features are the stated comparison, not a reported losing baseline. The activity leaves the direction and size of any F1 difference open.
Is a raw-force feature the same thing as a counterfactual force residual without impedance conditioning?

Not necessarily. ‘Raw-force features’ and ‘impedance-conditioned counterfactual force residuals’ name different representations. The activity specifies a comparison between them; it does not separately specify an unconditioned-residual variant. We should not treat raw-force features as though they isolate the effect of removing impedance conditioning alone.
Could that comparison prove that conditioning on impedance is the reason for any improvement?

For collaborative object transport, I’m proposing force-capped assistance micro-pauses to test whether a human correction persists without assistance. The robot would then confidence-gate control overrides using the observed response. How do these pieces fit together?

The micro-pause briefly changes the robot’s contribution so the human’s response can be observed without that assistance. If a correction continues, that may provide different evidence about intent than a correction that occurs only while assistance is present. The observed response would inform confidence in an intent interpretation, and that confidence would gate whether the robot overrides control. Force capping constrains the interaction during the proposed test. This is an approach to examine, not a claim that it already distinguishes the cases reliably.
What is the micro-pause testing, exactly?

It tests whether the human correction persists when the robot’s assistance is briefly paused. The question is whether the correction appears tied to the assistance or remains when that contribution is absent. Persistence can inform an interpretation of human intent, but the proposal does not make it a definitive test of what the person wants.
Does ‘without assistance’ mean the robot stops moving altogether?

Not necessarily. The proposal says to micro-pause assistance; it does not specify that all robot motion stops or describe the precise behavior during the pause. ‘Without assistance’ refers to the assistance whose effect on the human correction is being examined, not to a fully specified robot state.
Why call it a micro-pause rather than simply removing assistance?

‘Micro-pause’ conveys a brief interruption rather than an indefinite removal. Its role is to create an opportunity to observe the human response when assistance is not being applied. The proposal gives no duration, frequency, or rule for when a pause begins or ends.
If the correction persists through the pause, have we proved that the human changed route?

No. Persistence could make a changed intention more plausible, but it is not proof. The person may continue a movement for reasons that the brief observation does not resolve. The proposed use is to update confidence in an interpretation, not to equate every persistent correction with a route change.
And if the correction disappears when assistance is paused, is that proof it was just a reaction to the robot?

No. Its disappearance may be informative, but it does not uniquely establish a cause. A genuine change of intent might produce a response that is brief or that changes when the robot changes its contribution. The proposal asks the robot to use what it observes, while retaining uncertainty about what that response means.
So are we comparing the person’s behavior with assistance and during the pause?

Conceptually, yes. The robot observes a correction in the interaction and then examines whether it continues during a brief absence of assistance. That comparison brings the robot’s own contribution into the interpretation. The proposal does not specify a particular measurement, comparison formula, or behavioral threshold.
Would the pause tell us exactly what the human would have done if the robot had never assisted?

No. A brief pause occurs after the person has already interacted with the robot’s assistance. It provides an observed response to that pause, not a complete observation of an interaction in which the assistance had never occurred. That limits how strongly the response can be interpreted.
Does the proposal require every apparent human correction to trigger a micro-pause?

It does not give a triggering rule. Micro-pauses are the proposed way to test whether corrections persist without assistance, but the proposal does not specify when they are used or assert that every apparent correction receives one.
Could the micro-pause itself affect what the human does?

Yes, that is a possibility to keep in mind. Pausing assistance changes the interaction, so the observed response is a response under that changed condition. The proposal does not assume the pause is invisible to the person or that it reveals intent without influencing behavior.
Then why might the observation still be useful?

Because it provides information under a different assistance condition. A correction seen only while assistance is applied and a correction that continues during its pause are not identical observations. The difference could help the robot assess whether its own assistance is contributing to the correction, even though neither observation is conclusive on its own.
What exactly is meant by ‘observed response’ in the override rule?

It is the human response observed when assistance is micro-paused—particularly whether the correction persists without that assistance. The proposal does not specify which signals represent the response or how persistence is calculated. Its key point is that override confidence should draw on what happens during this brief test.
Is the observed response a direct measurement of the person’s intent?

No. It is observable behavior from which the robot may infer something about intent. The distinction matters: seeing a correction persist, change, or cease is not the same as directly knowing why the person acted that way.
How does confidence-gating affect a control override?

It makes confidence informed by the observed response relevant to whether an override occurs. Rather than treating the initial correction alone as sufficient grounds to take control, the robot would consider what the micro-pause reveals and how certain that makes its interpretation. The proposal does not supply a confidence calculation or a numerical gate threshold.
Does that mean a persistent correction automatically triggers an override?

No. Persistence is proposed evidence for interpreting the correction, while an override is a separate control action. Confidence-gating means the response informs that action; it does not say persistence alone is an automatic override command.
What if the response during the pause is ambiguous?
