The outcome concerns instances in which the robot overrides human control unnecessarily, not every override. The activity does not define the rule for judging an override unnecessary or specify whether the result will be expressed as a count, rate, or percentage.
Could fewer total overrides stand in for fewer unnecessary overrides?
No. Some overrides may be necessary. A change in the total number would not, on its own, tell us how the unnecessary subset changed. The named outcome is unnecessary control overrides.
Is the micro-pause itself necessarily an override?

Not as specified here. A micro-pause changes the robot’s assistance; an override is a control intervention being assessed as an outcome. The activity does not define each pause as an override or say that each pause leads to one.
How might intent-change F1 relate to the override outcome?

Intent inference can inform a control decision, but the outcomes remain separate. F1 assesses identification of changes in human intent, while the unnecessary-override measure assesses when the robot intervenes without need. A favorable F1 would not automatically establish fewer unnecessary overrides.
What distinction is the F1 meant to capture in collaborative transport?

It concerns identifying genuine changes in the human’s intent rather than mistaking corrections prompted by the robot’s assistance for such changes. F1 combines precision and recall for intent-change identification. The activity does not give a labeling procedure or separate precision and recall values.
If we obtain an F1 score, can I call it the percentage of genuine changes detected?
No. The percentage of genuine changes detected is recall. F1 combines recall with precision, so it should be reported as intent-change F1 rather than relabeled as a detection percentage or accuracy.
Does the activity require measuring F1 under fixed assistance as well as under rate-limited micro-pauses?

It calls for comparing the two approaches for intent-change F1, along with the other two outcomes. It does not specify how the intent labels are generated or scored under either condition, and it reports no score for either one.
Could fixed assistance serve as ground truth for what the human intended?

No. Fixed assistance is a control approach used as a comparator, not a definition of the human’s true intent. A comparison of F1 requires a basis for judging intent changes, but this activity does not specify how that basis is established.
Why include peak interaction force if unnecessary overrides are the main control concern?

Because taking control less often would not, by itself, show that the physical interaction remains acceptable. Peak force captures the highest reported interaction force under each approach. Comparing it separately prevents an override result from being treated as a force result.
Does ‘peak force’ refer to average force during the micro-pause?

No. Peak interaction force concerns a maximum, not an average. The activity does not restrict the peak measurement to the paused interval or specify how peaks are summarized across partners and trials.
If the approach has a lower reported peak than fixed assistance, can we say force was lower throughout every trial?
No. A lower peak would compare maxima as reported; it would not describe every moment of every interaction. This activity has not yet reported even the peak comparison.
Does a force limit or cap appear as a numerical setting in this activity?
No numerical force cap or rate-limit setting is stated. Peak force is an outcome to compare with fixed assistance, not a value supplied by the activity.
Is this crossover restricted to cases where an impedance switch and a route change happen simultaneously?

That restriction is not stated here. The activity specifies unseen-partner crossover trials, the two assistance approaches, and three outcomes. It does not provide a breakdown of switch or route-change timing conditions, so we should neither impose that restriction nor claim those cases are excluded.
Does the activity prescribe when the micro-pauses occur?
No. It does not give a pause trigger, schedule, frequency, or duration. Those implementation details should not be supplied as though they were part of this crossover activity.
Can I assume the two approaches are presented in randomized order?
No order or randomization rule is specified. ‘Crossover’ identifies the within-partner comparison, but it does not settle how the approaches are sequenced.
Do we know whether the same route is used under both approaches?
No path-matching rule is given. The activity establishes a crossover comparison, but it does not specify that the routes or every other feature of the interactions are identical between approaches.
Could this test demonstrate which individual component of rate-limited micro-pauses changes override behavior?

The stated comparison is between the rate-limited micro-pause approach and fixed assistance. It does not separately vary each component of the micro-pause approach, so any measured difference would belong to that comparison rather than automatically identifying one component as its cause.
Does the activity already show a reduction in unnecessary overrides?
No. It calls for comparing unnecessary overrides but provides no counts, rates, or reduction. The direction and size of the difference remain open.
Nor does it already show that intent-change F1 or peak force meets a particular target?
Correct. F1 and peak force are measures to be evaluated here. The activity supplies no scores or force values, so it establishes neither a classification threshold nor a force outcome.
If unnecessary overrides decrease but peak force increases, should I describe the test as an unqualified success?

No. That would be a mixed outcome across two of the named measures, and intent-change F1 would still need to be considered. The purpose of scoring all three is to keep override behavior, classification, and force from being collapsed into one judgment. No such outcome has been reported yet.
And if F1 improves while unnecessary overrides stay the same?

An improvement in intent-change identification would not establish an improvement in unnecessary overrides. The crossover measures both so they can be reported separately. At present, the activity does not say either change occurs.
Does testing on unseen partners mean the findings will apply to every future partner?

No. Unseen-partner trials address performance beyond partners used in the relevant training context, but they do not guarantee an outcome for every future person. The activity also gives no number of partners or trial results.
Can I call this a deployment test?

It is a crossover evaluation of rate-limited micro-pauses against fixed assistance on three specified outcomes. The activity does not authorize deployment or state that completing the trials automatically leads to it.
Please state the activity in one sentence without implying any of the three comparisons has been decided.

Run crossover trials with unseen partners comparing rate-limited micro-pauses and fixed assistance on unnecessary control overrides, intent-change F1, and peak interaction force; the outcomes remain to be measured.

The MicroPause crossover report records intent-change F1 of 0.86, 33% fewer unnecessary control overrides, and peak interaction force of 42 N versus 43 N for the baseline. How should I present the findings?

You can report that, in the unseen-partner crossover comparison of rate-limited micro-pauses with fixed assistance, the MicroPause report records intent-change F1 of 0.86 and 33% fewer unnecessary control overrides than fixed assistance. Reported peak interaction force was 42 N with rate-limited micro-pauses versus 43 N with the fixed-assistance baseline. The F1 value is reported for the micro-pause approach; the report does not give a fixed-assistance F1.
Which baseline does the 33% refer to?
Fixed assistance. The report says unnecessary control overrides were 33% fewer with rate-limited micro-pauses than with that baseline. It does not say that 33% of all overrides were unnecessary.
Can I calculate the number of unnecessary overrides avoided?
No. A 33% relative reduction does not reveal the underlying counts. The report does not provide the number of unnecessary overrides under either approach.
Does the finding say there were fewer overrides of every kind?
No. It specifically concerns unnecessary control overrides. The report does not give a total override count or say whether necessary overrides changed.
Is the 33% reduction an intent-change classification score?
No. It measures a difference in unnecessary control overrides relative to fixed assistance. Intent-change F1 of 0.86 is the separate classification result; neither number substitutes for the other.
What does F1 of 0.86 mean without turning it into a different metric?

It is an intent-change F1 score, which combines precision and recall for identifying changes in human intent. It is not an accuracy figure and does not, by itself, say what percentage of genuine intent changes were detected.
Can we tell whether false intent-change alarms or missed changes were more common?
No. The report gives F1 but does not give precision, recall, false-alarm counts, or missed-change counts separately. The score does not identify which kind of classification error predominated.
Is 0.86 also the F1 score for fixed assistance?

That is not stated. The report records intent-change F1 of 0.86 for the micro-pause approach, but it does not provide a baseline F1. The 33% override reduction and the 42 N versus 43 N peak-force comparison should not be mistaken for F1 comparisons.
So can I claim the micro-pause approach improved F1 over fixed assistance?
Not from this report alone. You can state the recorded intent-change F1 of 0.86, but an F1 improvement relative to fixed assistance requires its F1 score, which is not provided.
How should I assign the two peak-force numbers?
The reported peak is 42 N for rate-limited micro-pauses and 43 N for the fixed-assistance baseline. The peaks differ by 1 N, with the micro-pause approach lower in this comparison.
Is 42 N a force-cap setting or an observed outcome?

In the MicroPause crossover report, 42 N is the recorded peak interaction force. The report does not specify a numerical force-cap setting, so the measured peak should not be presented as a controller setting.
Does a 42 N peak mean the force was 42 N throughout every pause?
No. A peak is the highest reported interaction force, not a constant or average force. The report does not say when the peak occurred or describe the force trajectory during a pause.
Can I say the force was lower throughout the interaction with micro-pauses?
No. The report compares peak forces—42 N versus 43 N—not force at every moment. A lower reported peak does not establish a lower force throughout each interaction.
Is it fair to describe the reported peak as not increasing relative to fixed assistance?

Yes, if you keep the comparison limited to the reported peaks: 42 N for rate-limited micro-pauses is below 43 N for fixed assistance. That does not make a claim about every individual trial or every instant of interaction.
Does the 1 N difference tell us anything about average force?
No. Both numbers are peak interaction forces. The report supplies no average-force values for either approach.
What does ‘crossover’ let me say about the evaluation?

It identifies the report as arising from a comparison in which partners encounter both approaches. The activity associated with the report involved unseen partners. The report does not specify the order of conditions, the number of partners or trials, or how the reported outcomes were aggregated.
Can I assign the 0.86 F1, 33% reduction, and 42 N peak to every unseen partner?
No. Those are the reported crossover outcomes, not partner-by-partner results. The report supplies no individual F1 scores, override reductions, or peak-force values.
Does the name MicroPause tell us how long each pause lasted?

No duration is stated in this report. Its name identifies the report, while the recorded findings are the F1 score, relative reduction in unnecessary overrides, and two peak-force values. The pause duration should not be inferred from the name.
Can I say rate limiting alone caused the reduction in unnecessary overrides?

The report compares the rate-limited micro-pause approach with fixed assistance. It documents a 33% difference in unnecessary overrides between those approaches, but does not isolate rate limiting from other differences as the sole cause.
Does the report show that every override decision followed a correct interpretation of human intent?

No. An aggregate intent-change F1 and a reduction in unnecessary overrides do not establish that every individual classification or control decision was correct. The report gives no case-by-case account.
Could fewer unnecessary overrides be inferred just from the F1 score?

No. Here, the 33% reduction is a separately reported control outcome. Intent-change F1 concerns classification, while unnecessary overrides concern robot intervention. The report provides both measures rather than asking one to stand in for the other.
Do the findings show how often a human correction persisted when assistance was paused?
No. The report gives aggregate F1, override, and peak-force outcomes. It does not provide observations or counts of corrections that persisted or ceased during individual micro-pauses.
Can we say whether the differences are statistically significant?
No statistical test or uncertainty interval is included in the stated report. It is appropriate to give the recorded values and comparisons, but not to claim statistical significance from them alone.
Do these figures guarantee the same results for every future partner?
No. They describe the reported unseen-partner crossover comparison. They do not guarantee an F1 of 0.86, a 33% reduction, or peaks of 42 N and 43 N in every later interaction.
Please give me a concise results sentence that keeps all three measures and the baseline clear.

In the unseen-partner MicroPause crossover report, rate-limited micro-pauses recorded intent-change F1 of 0.86 and 33% fewer unnecessary control overrides than fixed assistance, with peak interaction force of 42 N versus 43 N for fixed assistance.

I’d like to propose learning partner-adaptive assistance-response kernels from low-amplitude impedance dithers. The robot would classify unexplained deviations as intent changes, then force-limit and confidence-gate its control overrides. How do those parts fit together?

The proposed kernels characterize how a partner responds to changes in the robot’s assistance. Low-amplitude impedance dithers provide robot-side changes from which to learn that response. The robot would compare subsequent behavior with what its learned assistance-response kernel explains and classify unexplained deviations as intent changes. Confidence-gating would govern whether that classification leads to a control override, while force-limiting would constrain the override’s physical effect. This is a proposed approach, not a demonstrated performance result.
What does ‘partner-adaptive’ mean here?

It means the assistance-response characterization is intended to adapt to the particular human partner rather than assume an identical response for everyone. The proposal does not specify when adaptation occurs, how much interaction it requires, or how the learned kernel is updated.
If the broader goal concerns unseen partners, does partner-adaptive imply the robot has already worked with each person?

No. A partner can be unseen before an interaction and still provide observations from which an adaptive approach might learn. The proposal does not say how quickly that learning happens or establish that it works for an unseen partner. ‘Partner-adaptive’ names the intended property, not a reported unseen-partner result.
What is an assistance-response kernel in plain English?

Here, it is a learned description of how a human partner’s observable response relates to the robot’s assistance. Its purpose is to help identify which later changes are plausibly reactions to the robot. The proposal does not define a particular mathematical kernel, response variable, or learning algorithm.
Does it have to be a specific mathematical kernel function?

No particular function is specified. You can call it an assistance-response kernel as the proposal does, while leaving its precise representation open. Writing down a particular equation or model structure would add an implementation choice.
What exactly is being dithered?

The robot’s impedance. The proposal calls for low-amplitude impedance dithers as the basis for learning the partner-adaptive assistance-response kernels. It does not specify the impedance values, the shape or frequency of the dithers, or how they are introduced.
Does ‘low-amplitude’ give us a numerical maximum?
No. It characterizes the dithers qualitatively but provides no numerical amplitude, unit, or range. A specific limit would need to be stated separately.
Is an impedance dither itself an observed human intent change?

No. The dither is a robot-side change. The human may respond to it, and that response is what the kernel is intended to characterize. Changing robot impedance does not itself establish that the human wants to change the transport route.
Why introduce a dither instead of just watching the person under unchanged assistance?

A deliberate, low-amplitude change in robot impedance can provide information about how the person responds to a change originating with the robot. That is relevant when a later correction could be a reaction to assistance rather than a change of intent. The proposal does not establish how informative the dithers will be or claim that observation under unchanged assistance would be useless.
Can I call the dither a direct test of what the person intends?
Not directly. It is a way to probe the partner’s response to robot assistance. An observed response remains behavior that needs interpretation; it is not direct access to the person’s intention.
Could the dither itself prompt the partner to correct their movement?

It could. Indeed, observing responses to changes in assistance is relevant to the proposed learning step. But the proposal does not specify what response any partner will produce or assume that introducing a low-amplitude dither leaves their behavior unaffected.
Does low amplitude guarantee the dither is imperceptible or harmless?

No. ‘Low-amplitude’ alone establishes neither that a person cannot perceive it nor any measured safety outcome. The proposal also calls for force-limiting overrides, but gives no measured forces or guarantee about the effects of the dithers themselves.
What is the kernel supposed to explain during collaborative object transport?

It is intended to explain observable deviations that arise as a partner responds to the robot’s assistance. If a correction is consistent with such a response, the robot has a reason not to treat it automatically as changed human intent. The proposal does not specify the observations used or claim that the kernel explains every assistance-induced correction.
Does that make every deviation the kernel cannot explain a genuine intent change?

That is the proposed classification rule: classify unexplained deviations as intent changes. But a classification is not proof of the human’s underlying intent. A deviation might also be unexplained because the learned response is incomplete or the observation is ambiguous. The proposal needs evaluation rather than assuming every such classification is correct.
Should I soften the proposal to say the robot merely considers an unexplained deviation and never classifies it?

That would change what is proposed. The stated approach does classify unexplained deviations as intent changes. The careful qualification is that this classification is an inference, not a guaranteed fact, and that a separate confidence gate governs control overrides.
What would count as ‘unexplained’ without inventing a numerical threshold?

Conceptually, it means the observed deviation is not adequately accounted for by the learned assistance-response kernel. The proposal does not specify how adequacy is measured, what size of deviation qualifies, or whether any particular signal is compared. Those remain implementation questions.
Is an unexplained deviation necessarily a change in route?

The broader intent distinction during object transport can involve the human wanting a different route, but the proposal says to classify unexplained deviations as intent changes. It does not establish that every unexplained movement corresponds to a particular route change, nor define a separate route-change labeling rule.
What if the person changes their intent and also reacts to the dither?

Both influences could be present in an interaction. The kernel is meant to account for response attributable to assistance, while the classification rule addresses what remains unexplained. The proposal does not guarantee that the two influences can be perfectly separated in an individual case.
Could the kernel explain away a genuine intent change?

That is a possible classification risk. If observed behavior is treated as explainable by the assistance-response kernel when it actually includes changed intent, the approach could miss the change. The proposal does not report whether or how often that occurs.
And could it mark a reaction to assistance as unexplained?

Yes, if the learned kernel does not adequately capture that reaction, the deviation could be classified as an intent change under the proposed rule. That possibility is why the quality of the learned response matters; no accuracy or false-alarm result is provided here.
Is the kernel meant to predict force specifically?

The proposal calls it an assistance-response kernel and does not specify a force-only prediction or a particular measured signal. Force appears explicitly in the requirement to force-limit confidence-gated overrides. It would add an implementation detail to say the kernel necessarily predicts only forces.
Could we prescribe handle heading as the kernel’s sole input?
Not from this proposal. It does not specify the kernel’s inputs or outputs. Naming handle heading as its sole input would introduce a design decision not contained in the stated approach.
How does confidence-gating differ from the classification of an unexplained deviation?

Classification concerns the interpretation: the robot labels an unexplained deviation as a change of intent. Confidence-gating concerns the subsequent decision to override control. The proposal does not say that every classified change immediately triggers an override.
Does that mean the robot can label something an intent change but still not override?

Yes, that distinction is consistent with confidence-gated overrides. The proposal makes classification and intervention separate steps. It does not specify a confidence threshold or the exact behavior when confidence is insufficient.
If the classifier says ‘intent change,’ is its confidence automatically high?

No. Assigning a label does not imply certainty about it. The proposal specifically calls for confidence-gating overrides, so uncertainty in an intent-change classification remains relevant to the control decision.
Is the confidence gate based on how much of the deviation the kernel cannot explain?

That might be one way to think about confidence conceptually, but the proposal does not define its calculation. It says overrides should be confidence-gated, without specifying which quantities determine confidence or how they are combined.
Can I specify a confidence percentage that triggers an override?
No numerical confidence threshold is stated. Adding one would make a new control-design commitment rather than clarify the existing proposal.
Is force-limiting part of deciding whether the human intended a different route?

No. The kernel and the unexplained-deviation classification address intent inference. Confidence-gating governs intervention, and force-limiting constrains the physical effect of overrides. Keeping these roles distinct avoids treating a force constraint as evidence about human intent.
What is being force-limited: every robot action or specifically the gated overrides?
The proposal specifically says to force-limit confidence-gated overrides. It does not describe a force limit for every robot action or give an implementation for other parts of the interaction.
Does ‘force-limit’ specify a peak force of 43 N?
No numerical force limit is included in this proposal. The wording does not assign 43 N, or any other value, to these overrides. Nor does specifying a limit provide a measured peak interaction force.
Could I claim force-limited overrides cannot increase peak interaction forces?

Not from the proposal alone. Force-limiting is intended to constrain the interaction, but whether peak interaction forces increase relative to a comparison condition is an empirical outcome. No force measurements or comparison are reported here.
Does confidence-gating guarantee fewer unnecessary control overrides?

No. It is a proposed way to make overrides selective, but the proposal gives no override count or reduction. In particular, it does not establish the broader target of 30% fewer unnecessary overrides relative to fixed assistance.
And does classifying unexplained deviations establish intent-change F1 ≥0.85 on unseen partners?

No. That is a broader performance target, not an outcome reported for this proposal. Whether the partner-adaptive kernels support that F1 for unseen partners when assistance itself induces corrections would need to be assessed.
Could the adaptation make the approach work for every partner by definition?

No. Being designed to adapt does not guarantee that the learned kernel captures every individual’s response or that it adapts sufficiently quickly. The proposal gives no per-partner performance result or universal guarantee.
Are the impedance dithers necessarily continuous throughout transport?

The proposal does not specify when or how often they occur. It says to learn kernels from low-amplitude impedance dithers; a continuous schedule, an occasional schedule, or a triggering rule would be an additional design detail.
Does it say the robot must finish learning the kernel before it can transport an object?

No. It does not specify the sequence between learning and transport, or when a kernel becomes usable. It identifies a source of information for a partner-adaptive response model without committing to a training timetable.
Would a change in the partner’s reaction over time invalidate the proposal?

The proposal does not make that judgment. ‘Partner-adaptive’ suggests the response description is intended to reflect the partner, but it does not specify how changes over time would be handled or whether any particular change would defeat the approach.
What can I safely say the low-amplitude dithers contribute?

They are the proposed means of learning how a partner responds to robot assistance through changes in robot impedance. Their role is informational: they help establish what assistance-related deviations might look like. The proposal supplies no quantitative characterization of the dithers or evidence that they reliably elicit identifiable responses.
What if there is no deviation after a dither?

That would be an observation, but the proposal does not prescribe how the kernel handles it or what it implies about later corrections. We should not infer that an absent observable response means the partner will never react to assistance.
Could we say the robot compares an observed correction against its expectation for that specific partner?

Yes, as a conceptual paraphrase. The partner-adaptive assistance-response kernel provides an expectation about reactions to assistance, and the robot classifies deviations that the kernel cannot explain as intent changes. The proposal does not specify an exact comparison formula or a numerical decision boundary.
Does an override follow merely because a deviation is unusual for that partner?

Not automatically. An unexplained deviation is proposed to be classified as an intent change, but an override remains confidence-gated and force-limited. Being unusual is not, by itself, a fully specified control rule.
Is this a proposal to reduce the human’s influence over the object whenever the robot is uncertain?

No. The proposal says to confidence-gate overrides using the intent inference, not to override whenever uncertainty rises. It does not define what the robot does in every uncertain case, so it should not be described as routinely taking more control when unsure.
How do I explain the intended benefit without claiming it has happened?

You can say the approach aims to avoid confusing predictable responses to robot assistance with genuine human intent changes, and to make control overrides conditional on confidence while constraining their forces. Those are motivations for the proposed mechanisms, not evidence that classification, override, or peak-force targets have been achieved.
Please put the proposal in one sentence, preserving all of its parts.

Propose learning partner-adaptive assistance-response kernels from low-amplitude robot impedance dithers, classifying deviations the kernels cannot explain as human intent changes, and confidence-gating control overrides while force-limiting them.

I want to calibrate the partner-adaptive assistance-response kernels with ±5% robot impedance dithers, then evaluate unseen-partner intent-change F1, unnecessary-override reduction, and peak interaction force against fixed assistance. How should I describe this plan?

Describe it as two planned stages: use ±5% impedance dithers to calibrate the assistance-response kernels, then evaluate the resulting approach with unseen partners against fixed assistance. Keep the three outcomes distinct: intent-change F1 measures identification of changed human intent, unnecessary-override reduction measures control intervention, and peak interaction force measures the physical interaction. The plan reports no results for any of them.
What does the ±5% value apply to?
It applies to the robot impedance dithers used for kernel calibration. It does not describe an intended change in human behavior, an F1 tolerance, an override-reduction target, or a force limit.
Is that five percentage points of impedance?

No. The stated quantity is ±5% impedance dithers. ‘Percentage points’ would be appropriate for a difference between two percentages, such as two measured override rates; it is not a clearer way to express this dither magnitude.
Can we give the actual impedance values corresponding to ±5%?
Not from this plan. It does not specify the reference impedance or its units, so the dither should remain expressed as ±5% rather than converted into absolute impedance values.
Does ±5% tell us the waveform or how often the impedance changes?
No. It specifies the dither magnitude but not its timing, frequency, waveform, number of applications, or scheduling during transport.
What does calibrating an assistance-response kernel mean at this level?

It means using the partner’s observed response to those robot-side impedance changes to establish the kernel’s description of responses to assistance. The kernel is intended to help distinguish behavior explainable as a reaction to the robot from a potential change in human intent. The plan does not specify a mathematical representation, calibration algorithm, or criterion for adequate calibration.
Are the impedance dithers intended to make the human change route?

That is not the stated purpose. The dithers change robot impedance so the system can characterize responses to its assistance. A robot-side impedance change is not itself a human intent change, and the plan does not claim it induces any particular route decision.
Could a partner correct their motion in response to a dither?

That is possible and is relevant to learning how the partner reacts to changes in robot assistance. But the plan does not predict a particular correction or say that every dither will produce an observable response.
Does calibrating a kernel prove it explains every assistance-induced correction?

No. Calibration is a planned procedure, not proof that all later human responses will match the kernel. The evaluation is needed to examine how well the resulting approach distinguishes intent changes when interacting with unseen partners.
Does ‘partner-adaptive’ mean we must calibrate a separate kernel in advance for every unseen partner?

The plan does not say how adaptation to a partner is scheduled or whether calibration occurs before or during that partner’s evaluation. It calls for calibrating response kernels with ±5% dithers and evaluating on unseen partners. A procedure that exposes held-out evaluation responses during model selection should not be silently assumed from those words.
Could we call the evaluation leave-one-partner-out?

Not from this plan alone. ‘Unseen partners’ specifies the population on which performance should be evaluated; it does not prescribe a leave-one-partner-out split or another particular evaluation design.
Why is testing with unseen partners important for this approach?

Because a response pattern learned from particular people may not describe how someone new reacts to assistance. Unseen-partner evaluation asks whether the calibrated approach supports the intent distinction and control outcomes beyond partners already encountered in the relevant preparation. The plan does not say how many such partners are included.
What is the difference between intent-change F1 and override reduction here?

Intent-change F1 assesses whether the system identifies changed human intent rather than misreading a reaction to robot assistance. Override reduction assesses how often the robot unnecessarily takes control relative to fixed assistance. A good classification score does not automatically establish fewer unnecessary overrides, so both are named outcomes.
Is intent-change F1 just the percentage of real route changes it catches?

No. That percentage would be recall. F1 combines precision and recall, accounting both for missed genuine changes and for incorrect indications of changed intent. The plan calls for evaluating F1 but gives no score or separate precision and recall values.
Could we infer intent-change F1 from how often a kernel says a deviation is unexplained?

No. The frequency of unexplained deviations is not an F1 score. F1 requires assessing intent-change classifications against the relevant intent labels, including mistaken indications and missed changes. The plan does not specify how those reference labels are assigned.
In the proposed method, are unexplained deviations still treated as intent changes?

That is the proposed interpretation for the kernel-based approach. The calibration plan does not establish that every unexplained deviation truly reflects changed intent. Evaluating intent-change F1 is a way to measure how well the interpretation works in the stated setting.
Does fixed assistance define the true human intent for scoring F1?

No. Fixed assistance is the comparison approach, not ground truth for human intent. The plan does not specify a reference-labeling procedure, so the comparator should not be described as supplying the correct answer for each human response.
What does ‘evaluate override reduction against fixed assistance’ mean without specifying counts?

It means assess whether the kernel-based approach produces fewer unnecessary control overrides than the fixed-assistance baseline. The plan provides neither the baseline count nor an observed reduction, so it cannot establish an absolute number of avoided overrides or a measured percentage.
Does it ask us to eliminate all overrides?
No. The outcome is reduction of unnecessary overrides. Some overrides could be appropriate; the plan does not require eliminating every intervention or define all overrides as unnecessary.
Can I assume the confidence gate has a numerical threshold already?
No. The associated proposal calls for confidence-gated, force-limited overrides, but this plan specifies no confidence calculation, threshold, or exact mapping from intent inference to an override.
Will the kernel’s intent classification necessarily cause an override?

Not necessarily. Classification and control intervention are separate. An unexplained deviation may be classified as an intent change under the proposed approach, while an override remains subject to confidence gating. The plan evaluates both identification and unnecessary overrides without equating them.
What is peak interaction force measuring?

It measures the highest interaction force in the assessed interaction, rather than an average force. Evaluating it alongside override reduction matters because fewer unnecessary overrides would not by itself establish that peak forces remain controlled.
Does ±5% impose a bound on peak interaction force?
No. The ±5% value describes the impedance dither magnitude used for calibration. It is not a force value or a measured peak. The plan separately calls for evaluating peak interaction force.
Is a numerical force cap specified for the overrides in this plan?

No numerical cap is given here. The broader kernel-based proposal calls for force-limited confidence-gated overrides, while this plan requires peak-force evaluation against fixed assistance. Neither statement supplies a cap value or an observed force peak.
What does comparing peak force against fixed assistance let us assess?

It lets us assess whether the approach’s reported peak interaction force differs from the fixed-assistance baseline’s peak under the planned evaluation. The plan does not state either value, so it cannot establish an increase, a decrease, or equality.
If intent-change F1 is strong, can we skip measuring peak force?

No. Classification performance does not determine the highest physical interaction force. The plan explicitly names both outcomes, along with override reduction, because each addresses a different question.
And if the peak force is low, can we conclude the intent classifier works?
No. A force outcome does not tell us whether the robot interpreted the human’s corrections correctly. Intent-change F1 must be evaluated separately.
Does the plan contain a result for any of these three outcomes?
No. Calibrating with ±5% impedance dithers and evaluating on unseen partners are proposed activities. The plan supplies no intent-change F1 score, override-reduction figure, or peak-force value.
Can I relate the measures to the shared-control goal without claiming success?

Yes. The goal seeks intent-change F1 ≥0.85 for unseen partners when robot assistance induces human corrections, plus 30% fewer unnecessary overrides than fixed assistance without increased peak interaction forces. This plan identifies corresponding evaluations for the kernel-based approach. It does not say those thresholds or the force condition have been achieved.
Does this plan explicitly say every evaluation trial includes an assistance-induced correction?

No. It names unseen-partner intent F1, override reduction, and peak force against fixed assistance, but does not give a detailed trial-condition breakdown. The broader intent distinction motivates the evaluation; a claim that every trial contains a specific correction would add an unstated design detail.

I’d like to propose fusing anticipatory gaze and torso orientation with handle forces to identify route changes before assistance-induced corrections, then confidence-gating force-limited control overrides. How do those parts fit together?

The proposed inference combines cues about where the human may be preparing to go—anticipatory gaze and torso orientation—with the forces at the handle. The aim is to identify a genuine change in intended route before a correction prompted by the robot’s assistance complicates its interpretation. Confidence in that inference would then govern whether the robot overrides control, and any such override would be force-limited. This is a proposed approach, not a reported result.
What makes gaze ‘anticipatory’ in this description?

It refers to gaze as a possible early indication of a route the person intends to take, rather than treating gaze only as a reaction after the object has moved. The proposal does not define a gaze direction, observation interval, or rule for deciding that a particular glance is anticipatory.
Does looking toward a route prove the person wants the object to go that way?

No. Gaze can provide evidence relevant to an intent inference, but a look alone does not establish a route change. The proposal combines it with torso orientation and handle forces rather than declaring any single glance decisive.
What does torso orientation contribute?

It is another proposed cue to how the human is orienting during the shared transport task. Considering it alongside gaze and handle forces may help assess whether an observed movement reflects a change in intended route. The proposal does not state that torso orientation always leads movement or specify how it is measured.
Could torso orientation also change because the person is correcting for the robot?

Yes, that remains a possible interpretation. An orientation change is observable behavior, not a direct readout of intent. The proposed fusion is meant to help distinguish route changes from assistance-induced corrections, not to assume that every change in posture is intentional rerouting.
Why include handle forces if gaze and torso orientation might give early cues?

Handle forces provide information about the physical interaction during collaborative transport. They can be considered together with gaze and torso orientation instead of relying only on a bodily cue or only on force. Because robot assistance can itself affect the forces and elicit corrections, handle forces still require interpretation.
Does a change in handle force automatically mean the human changed route?

No. The force can reflect the coupled human–robot interaction, including a reaction to the robot’s assistance. The proposal is to fuse force information with anticipatory gaze and torso orientation to infer a route change, not to equate any force change with one.
What does ‘fuse’ mean without specifying an algorithm?

It means using the three types of information together in the intent inference, rather than assessing each in isolation. The proposal does not specify a model architecture, weighting, calculation, or decision threshold for combining them.
Do all three cues have to agree before the robot can identify a change?

That rule is not stated. Fusion does not necessarily mean unanimous agreement, and the proposal does not prescribe how conflicting cues are handled. A disagreement would be relevant to uncertainty, but no specific inference rule is supplied.
Suppose gaze suggests another route but the handle force does not change. Can we label that an intent change?

The proposal does not give a rule for that case. It would be premature to treat a gaze cue alone as a definite route change or to dismiss it solely because force has not changed. The point of combining cues is to form an interpretation whose confidence can be considered before an override.
And if the handle forces change while gaze and torso orientation do not?

That, too, could have more than one explanation, including a reaction to assistance. The proposal does not assign a fixed label to that pattern. Its intended distinction is between a genuine route change and a correction elicited by the robot, using the cues together.
What does ‘before assistance-induced corrections’ require?

It sets a temporal aim for identifying the route change: use the anticipatory and interaction cues early enough that the inference is not based solely on a later correction induced by the robot’s assistance. It does not give a time limit in milliseconds or claim that every route change can be recognized before any correction occurs.
Does that mean the robot must identify a change before it ever assists?

No. The proposal concerns shared transport in which assistance can induce corrections. ‘Before assistance-induced corrections’ concerns the relative timing of the intended identification and those corrections; it does not say the robot must refrain from assistance or finish all intent inference before providing any.
Could the robot’s assistance affect gaze or torso orientation as well as handle forces?

That is possible in a human–robot interaction. The proposal does not declare either bodily cue immune to the robot’s influence. Calling gaze anticipatory states why it might be useful for earlier inference, not that it always reflects intent independently of assistance.
If a person truly changes route after an assistance-induced correction begins, is that ruled out?

No. The proposal aims to identify route changes before assistance-induced corrections complicate the interpretation, but it does not assert that human intent cannot change later. It also does not prescribe a separate procedure for every ordering of a correction and a genuine route change.
Is an assistance-induced correction necessarily an error by the human?

No. It is a human response to what the robot is doing, and it may be an appropriate correction. The concern is whether the robot mistakenly interprets that response as a new intended route, not whether the person’s correction is wrong.
Does this approach classify route changes, or does it only choose when to take control?

Both functions are present but distinct. Fusing gaze, torso orientation, and handle forces is proposed for identifying route changes. Confidence-gating governs the later choice to override control, and force-limiting constrains an override if one occurs.
What does confidence-gating an override mean here?

It means confidence in the inferred route change matters to whether the robot overrides control. An observed cue or even a tentative intent-change classification should not automatically produce an override. The proposal gives no numerical confidence threshold or complete control rule.
If the cues indicate a route change confidently, must the robot override?

Not as stated. Confidence-gating makes confidence relevant to the override decision; it does not say every confident inference requires intervention. Identification of intent and the need for an override remain different questions.
What if the gaze, torso, and handle cues are contradictory?

That could leave the intent inference uncertain. The confidence gate is intended to prevent a poorly supported inference from automatically driving a control override, but the proposal does not specify how confidence is calculated or exactly what action the robot takes when cues conflict.
Does the force limit apply to the inference or to the control action?

It applies to the proposed control overrides. Handle forces are an input to intent inference; force-limiting is a constraint on the override’s physical interaction. They should not be treated as the same function merely because both involve force.
Is there a particular force limit in newtons?
No numerical force limit is specified in this proposal. It calls for force-limited overrides, but does not state a cap value or report an observed peak interaction force.
Does force-limiting an override establish that peak interaction forces cannot rise?

No. It proposes a constraint, not a measured comparison. Whether peak interaction forces increase under the approach would have to be assessed; the proposal does not establish an outcome relative to fixed assistance.
Would fusing the cues necessarily reduce unnecessary control overrides?

No. Earlier or more informative intent inference and confidence-gating may be intended to make overrides more selective, but neither mechanism supplies an override count. The proposal reports no percentage reduction in unnecessary overrides.
Can we say it achieves intent-change F1 ≥0.85 for unseen partners?

No. That is a performance objective for the shared-control robot, not a reported result for this proposed fusion. The proposal does not specify an unseen-partner evaluation or give an intent-change F1 score.
What about the 30% override-reduction target versus fixed assistance?

That remains a separate outcome to evaluate. The proposal calls for confidence-gated, force-limited overrides but provides no comparison showing 30% fewer unnecessary overrides than fixed assistance or establishing that peak interaction forces do not increase.
Could a strong intent-change classifier still lead to unnecessary overrides?

Yes, conceptually. A classification summarizes what the robot infers, while an override is a control action. That is why the proposal includes confidence-gating rather than treating classification performance as sufficient to establish appropriate intervention.
Would an override with limited force necessarily be necessary?

No. Force-limiting constrains the physical effect of an override; it does not determine whether intervening was warranted. Confidence-gating addresses whether to override, while the force limit addresses the interaction if an override occurs.
Can I characterize the fusion as proving which signal reflects intent and which reflects assistance?

No. The approach proposes using their combined evidence to make a distinction. It does not prove that any individual gaze movement, torso rotation, or handle-force change has a unique cause, or that the proposed cues perfectly separate all corrections from route changes.
Does the proposal require cameras, wearable sensors, or a specific handle design?

It names gaze, torso orientation, and handle forces as information to fuse, but specifies no sensors or hardware for obtaining them. Assigning a particular sensing arrangement would add an implementation decision.
Does it say how long a gaze or torso change has to persist?

No. It provides no angular thresholds, persistence durations, sampling rates, or timing window for the cues. The temporal point stated is the aim to identify route changes before assistance-induced corrections.
Could you give a conceptual illustration without implying that any cue pattern has been validated?

Conceptually, the robot could consider whether gaze and torso orientation suggest a route change before interpreting a subsequent handle-force correction. If the force correction might instead be a response to assistance, the earlier cues could provide context. That illustrates the proposed distinction; it is not a prescribed classifier rule or evidence that the approach works.
What is the central uncertainty the proposal leaves open?

Whether combining those cues actually identifies genuine route changes early and reliably when the robot’s assistance can induce human corrections. It also leaves open whether confidence-gated overrides reduce unnecessary interventions and whether force-limiting prevents an increase in peak interaction forces. No performance results are stated.
Please state the full proposal in one sentence, keeping inference, overrides, and force control separate.

Propose fusing anticipatory gaze and torso orientation with handle forces to identify human route changes before assistance-induced corrections, then confidence-gating control overrides and force-limiting any overrides that occur.

What does ‘override reduction’ measure separately from F1?

It concerns how often the robot overrides human control under the adopted approach compared with fixed assistance. F1 concerns the correctness of intent-change identification. Is the outcome explicitly limited to unnecessary overrides?

If the robot produces a false intent-change alarm, is an unnecessary override certain to follow?

Could the override reduction be calculated before counting the fixed-assistance overrides?

No measured relative reduction can be calculated without outcomes for the comparison. This activity names fixed assistance as the comparator but supplies no override counts or rates for either approach.
Why measure peak interaction force as well?

A change in intent-change F1 or override frequency does not establish what happens to the highest physical interaction force. Peak force is therefore scored separately for the adopted approach and fixed assistance. No measured peaks are supplied here.
Is peak force an average of force during the MicroPause fallback?
No. Peak interaction force refers to a maximum in the assessed interaction, not an average. The activity does not limit its measurement to fallback periods or say when a peak might occur.
Does using a force-limited fallback guarantee a lower peak than fixed assistance?
No. A force constraint in an approach is not a measured comparison. The trials are intended to assess peak interaction force rather than assume its relationship to fixed assistance.
Can I fill in a numerical force cap or a peak from a different report?
No. This activity specifies no numerical cap or measured peak. Results from another assessment should not be presented as observations from these mixed-visibility crossovers.
Could this test address the goal of F1 ≥0.85 and 30% fewer unnecessary overrides without increased peak force?

Would exceeding an F1 threshold compensate for an increase in peak force?
No. Classification and physical force are distinct outcomes. Likewise, a favorable peak-force comparison would not by itself establish either F1 performance or override reduction.
Does this activity tell us whether gaze and torso cues individually account for any improvement?

Could a favorable overall F1 mean the quality gate selected the right mode on every trial?

Does completing the crossover automatically establish that the robot is ready for deployment?

No. Running a trial is not itself a performance result or a deployment decision. This activity calls for measuring three outcomes against fixed assistance on unseen partners; it does not specify a deployment rule.
